message.content:
I don’t have real‑time access to current air‑quality data, so I can’t tell you the exact AQI for Los Angeles at this moment. However, here’s what you can do to get up‑to‑date information:

| Source | How to use |
|--------|------------|
| **AirNow** (U.S. EPA) | Visit <https://www.airnow.gov/> and enter “Los Angeles” or your ZIP code. It shows the current AQI, pollutant breakdowns, and health advisories. |
| **AQICN** (World Air Quality Index) | Go to <https://aqicn.org/city/los-angeles/>. It provides a live AQI, forecast, and historical data. |
| **Weather apps** (e.g., Weather.com, AccuWeather, or your phone’s weather widget) | Many include an AQI indicator for major cities. |
| **Local news** | TV or online news outlets often report on air‑quality alerts during smog events. |

If you’re looking for a quick snapshot, you can also try a voice assistant (Google Assistant, Siri, Alexa) and ask, “What’s the air quality in Los Angeles?” They usually pull from one of the above services.

---

### Quick reference (typical values)

| AQI Category | Health Impact |
|--------------|---------------|
| 0–50 (Good) | No adverse health effects. |
| 51–100 (Moderate) | Sensitive groups may experience mild effects. |
| 101–150 (Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups) | People with respiratory or heart conditions may feel symptoms. |
| 151–200 (Unhealthy) | Everyone may experience health effects. |
| 201–300 (Very Unhealthy) | Serious health effects; avoid prolonged outdoor activity. |
| 301–500 (Hazardous) | Avoid all outdoor activity; immediate health risks. |

Feel free to let me know if you’d like a deeper dive into specific pollutants (PM₂.₅, ozone, etc.) or how to interpret the numbers!
